strengths: Introduces the first real-world camera-based aerial 3D semantic scene completion benchmark, filling a clear gap in an under-explored domain.
Provides a substantial dataset with 9 scenes, over 20,000 samples, 22 semantic classes, multi-altitude imagery (30/40/50 m), multiple seasons, and urban/industrial/rural scenarios.

Proposes a LiDAR-free image-based data generation pipeline that leverages SfM/MVS and 2D-to-3D label lifting, reducing manual annotation effort to <10% of images while covering >99% of reconstructed points.
Includes detailed benchmark experiments with altitude-wise, class-wise, and group-wise analyses, plus extensive supplementary material on implementation and qualitative results.
Promises release of code and dataset, which would enhance reproducibility and support future research on aerial semantic scene completion.
weaknesses: Only one SSC method (CGFormer) is benchmarked; broader comparisons with other camera-based SSC methods such as MonoScene, TPVFormer, or VoxFormer would substantially strengthen the benchmark evidence.

Ground-truth label quality is not quantitatively validated; reprojection RMSE and qualitative examples do not establish semantic/occupancy accuracy, particularly for Poisson-based ground densification and visual-hull instance carving.

Dataset spatial coverage is limited to about 194,000 m² across 9 scenes in a single geographic region, and comparisons to terrestrial benchmarks based on sample/voxel counts may overstate scene diversity and scale.
The static-scene assumption suppresses dynamic objects and can cause inconsistent labels across views/altitudes; temporal inconsistencies are acknowledged but not quantified.
Extreme class imbalance (e.g., Building 75.7%, many classes <0.01%) may make mIoU unreliable and dominated by rare classes, affecting benchmark utility.

Reproducibility is limited at review time because the dataset and code are not yet available, and key details such as the collection location and full annotation protocol are withheld or only promised.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: SSC has been studied almost exclusively from terrestrial viewpoints, and the paper introduces what appears to be the first real-world aerial SSC benchmark. The domain (low-altitude UAV perception) is well-motivated by practical constraints (flight regulations, mass/energy limits, LiDAR sparsity at elevated viewpoints).

Substantial and well-documented dataset: 9 scenes, 20,160 annotated samples, ~193,938 m², 22 semantic classes, three altitudes (30/40/50 m), four seasons, and urban/industrial/rural scenarios, with 5× the samples and 6× the labeled voxels of SemanticKITTI (Tables 1–3). Voxel grids follow the SSCBench organization (192×128×128, r=0.5 m), enabling seamless integration with existing SSC codebases.

The LiDAR-free, camera-centric data-generation framework is a real methodological contribution. By exploiting SfM+MVS 2D–3D correspondences (Eq. 1–3), manual annotation of <10% of images suffices to label >99% of reconstructed points (ρ(L) > 0.99), which is a practical answer to the annotation bottleneck for aerial data.

Careful ground-truth construction: class-aware densification (DBSCAN instance separation with per-class parameters, Poisson surface reconstruction for ground classes, silhouette-based voxel carving for instances), explicit conflict-resolution precedence (Eq. 13), and per-frame frustum culling with invalid/surface/occluded masks mirroring SemanticKITTI (Eq. 14, Sec. 3.3.4). The design is principled rather than ad hoc.

Useful auxiliary modality: per-frame metric depth maps (20,160) are provided and their value is demonstrated by fine-tuning Depth Anything V2, with consistent gains across all three altitudes (Table 4), plus a cross-domain zero-shot transfer study to V-KITTI-2 (Table 10). This shows the dataset has downstream utility beyond a single task.

Reproducibility is well supported: code is promised, dataset to be released, and the supplement documents DBSCAN hyperparameters (Table 5), per-scene annotation ratios (Table 8, avg. 9.17%), per-scene reprojection errors (Table 7, 0.39–2.61 px), image-overlap maps (Fig. 9, >90%), and depth histograms (Fig. 7).
Writing is clear and the pipeline is presented chronologically with a helpful overview figure; class/group/altitude-wise evaluation (Fig. 3) is a sensible diagnostic breakdown.
weaknesses: The semantic ground truth is not directly validated. Only geometric proxies are reported (mean RMS reprojection error 1.24 px, point-coverage ρ(L) > 0.99). Since labels are propagated by majority voting, kNN with inverse-distance weighting, a second kNN denoising pass, and heuristic densification, systematic semantic errors are plausible, and no independent check (e.g., manual verification of voxel labels, held-out annotation, or comparison against any LiDAR/independent reference) is provided. For a dataset paper this is the most consequential gap.

Severe class imbalance undercuts the 22-class taxonomy: Building accounts for 75.75% and Roof 1.74%, while Person (0.0002%), Flying Animal (0.0001%), Cable (0.0017%), Cable Tower (0.0040%), Crane (0.0052%) are essentially unpopulated (Table 6). Because mIoU is averaged over non-empty classes, evaluation is dominated by a few classes, and the class-wise conclusions in Fig. 3 and Table 11 for rare classes are statistically fragile.

The benchmark evaluation is thin for a paper whose headline claim is a 'comprehensive vision benchmark': only one SSC method (CGFformer) is evaluated, with no comparison to other recent baselines (e.g., VoxFormer, TPVFormer, Symphonies, SOAP, OccFormer) and no ablation isolating the effect of the data-generation design choices (densification, voxel carving, mask definitions). The paper's own observation that existing SSC architectures are 'not yet optimized for this regime' would be much stronger with more than a single model.

The pipeline depends on very high image overlap (>90%) and dense double-grid flight patterns; it is unclear how it degrades in texture-poor, reflective, or vegetated regions. Moreover, the class-aware densification heuristics (Poisson surface reconstruction for ground classes, visual-hull carving for instances) can synthesize occupancy in regions that were never observed, potentially inflating ground truth. No quantification of how often this occurs, or of its effect on metrics, is given.

Static-scene assumption and temporal inconsistency: dynamic objects are suppressed and cross-altitude captures may be temporally inconsistent (acknowledged in Sec. 6). Instance classes such as Person and Vehicle are nearly absent in practice, so the dataset cannot support dynamic or temporally consistent aerial SSC, limiting its scope relative to the stated 'holistic' ambition.

Geographic and scene diversity is limited: the data come from a single geographic region, scene locations are withheld, and there are only 9 scenes. The urban/industrial/rural coverage claim rests on a small sample, and generalization to other cities, terrain, or sensor platforms is untested.

Presentation issue: in Sec. 9.2 the text states that the proposed model 'outperforms the baseline in metric-sensitive measures,' but the tabulated AbsRel/RMSE (1.098/16.711 for DAv2-OccuFly on V-KITTI-2 vs. 0.729/28.369 for DAv2-metric on OccuFly) do not straightforwardly support that reading. The cross-domain argument is stated in a way that is difficult to follow.

Minor: the 'first' claims (first real-world aerial SSC benchmark, largest aerial metric depth dataset) are plausible but rest on comparisons with a relatively small set of prior aerial datasets (Tables 2, 3, 9); a broader survey of UAV datasets would strengthen the positioning.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: no dedicated real-world (or synthetic) aerial SSC benchmark existed, and OccuFly is a credible first attempt at a real-world aerial 3D semantic scene completion benchmark, which is a useful target for UAV autonomy.

Substantial scale and diversity relative to the target domain: 9 scenes, 20,160 samples, ~194,000 m^2, 22 classes, three altitudes (50/40/30 m), four seasons, and urban/industrial/rural scenarios, with explicit comparison to SemanticKITTI (more samples and voxels).

The camera-based, LiDAR-free annotation pipeline is practically motivated (UAV flight regulations, mass/energy constraints, LiDAR sparsity at elevation) and the label-lifting scheme (annotating <10% of images to cover >99% of points) is an annotation-efficient design.
Provides per-frame metric depth maps and a fine-tuned DepthAnythingV2 model, with quantitative and qualitative depth evaluations, adding downstream utility beyond occupancy labels.
Adheres to established SSC data organization conventions (SSCBench-style voxel grids, invalid/surface/occluded binary masks), which aids integration and reproducibility.

Reproducibility signals are reasonable: code/dataset to be released, detailed hyperparameters (DBSCAN params, kNN settings, Poisson depth/scale, K=24 views), hardware, and quantitative reconstruction quality (avg RMS reprojection error 1.24 px).
weaknesses: The 'benchmark' deliverable is thin: only a single SSC method (CGFormer) is evaluated. For a benchmark paper, a multi-method evaluation (e.g., monocular, BEV/TPV, and voxel-based SSC methods) is expected; with one method, the benchmark does not yet establish a reliable ranking or a comparative signal.

No quantitative validation of the core methodological claim that lifted 3D labels are 'accurate per-point semantics.' Coverage (>99% of points observed) is reported, but coverage is not correctness; there is no precision/recall or confusion analysis against manually labeled 3D ground truth, and no error characterization of SfM+MVS/Poisson/kNN label transfer, especially in texture-poor regions the authors acknowledge are problematic.

The data generation 'framework' is largely a composition of well-established components (SfM+MVS, Poisson surface reconstruction, DBSCAN, kNN label transfer, silhouette-based voxel carving, frustum culling). The novelty is incremental, and no ablation or comparison against alternative design choices is provided to justify the specific pipeline.

The reported benchmark metrics appear degenerate: per-class IoU is 0.0000 for most classes, and mIoU is only ~0.008-0.014 (Table 11). Combined with near-zero-frequency classes (e.g., Flying Animal 0.0001%, Cable 0.0017%), this makes the benchmark's signal questionable and the mIoU statistic misleading. The paper attributes this entirely to task difficulty without diagnosing whether ground-truth alignment/quality also contributes.

Limited geographic and scene diversity: 9 scenes from a single, withheld geographic region. Generalization of the benchmark and the claimed 'scalable' framework to other regions/conditions is not demonstrated.

The pipeline assumes static scenes and may incur cross-altitude temporal inconsistencies (acknowledged in Sec. 6), but the magnitude and impact of these artifacts on label quality are neither measured nor bounded.
No comparison against synthetic aerial SSC data or baselines, so it is unclear how much added value the real-world dataset provides relative to cheaper synthetic alternatives for training/evaluation.

Some framing overstates novelty (e.g., 'first real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark' and 'novel and scalable data generation framework') relative to what is technically demonstrated; the contributions are more engineering integration than methodological advance.

strengths: Introduces the first real-world aerial semantic scene completion benchmark, addressing an underexplored domain with a camera-based, LiDAR-free data generation pipeline that fits UAV mass/energy constraints.

The annotation strategy is scalable and well justified: manually annotating <10% of 2D images and lifting labels to 3D via SfM+MVS multi-view correspondences yields >99% reconstructed-point coverage and 92% pixel-wise agreement on held-out manual annotations.

The dataset is substantial for a first aerial SSC benchmark: 9 scenes, 20,611 samples, 21 semantic classes, 193,938 m², 30/40/50 m altitudes, multiple seasons and urban/industrial/rural environments, with RGB images, semantic voxel grids, and 20,611 metric depth maps.

Benchmark experiments are informative: SOTA terrestrial SSC methods (Symphonies, DISC) and depth foundation models (MapAnything, Metric3Dv2, DepthAnything2/3) show severe aerial domain gaps, and fine-tuning depth models on OccuFly demonstrates the value of in-domain metric supervision.

The paper provides detailed implementation choices (DBSCAN parameters, silhouette carving, Poisson reconstruction, training protocols) and supplementary validation of reconstruction error, annotation ratios, class frequencies, and depth histograms, aiding reproducibility.
The benchmark is organized following SSCBench conventions, making it easy for existing SSC methods to integrate and encouraging future aerial SSC research.
weaknesses: Geographic diversity is limited: all nine scenes are collected in the Ingolstadt, Germany region. For a benchmark claiming aerial generalization, this may limit the ability to assess robustness across different cities, terrains, and building styles.

The ground truth assumes static scenes and does not explicitly handle dynamic objects; moving vehicles or pedestrians can create inconsistent labels or ghosting, as also acknowledged in the conclusion. This may introduce noise in otherwise carefully generated semantic voxel grids.

The semantic labels depend on SfM+MVS reconstruction and per-frame sampling from a 50 m scene-level semantic grid. Ground truth at 40 m and 30 m is frustum-culled from that grid rather than independently reconstructed/verified, so lower-altitude labels may inherit reconstruction errors and occlusions.

The exact dataset release plan is unclear in the provided manuscript: the abstract ends with 'Visit' and no URL/license/access information is given. For a benchmark paper, availability of data and code is critical for reproducibility and adoption.

Benchmark evaluation breadth is limited: only two SSC methods and a handful of depth models are tested. Many classes are extremely rare (e.g., person, bicycle, truck, crane) and reported mIoU is near zero, which may reduce the benchmark's immediate utility for long-tail semantic evaluation.

Some dataset statistics need clarification: Table 9 reports 6,393 acquired images and 586 annotated images, while Table 1 reports 20,611 total samples, making the relationship between acquired images, annotated images, and generated samples unclear in the main paper.

The depth benchmark uses MVS-derived depth maps as ground truth and then fine-tunes foundation models on OccuFly; independent depth validation beyond reprojection error is limited, and the circularity of using generated depth as both ground truth and training target deserves more discussion.

strengths: Introduces the first real-world camera-based aerial semantic scene completion benchmark, filling a clear gap between terrestrial SSC datasets and aerial/UAV applications.

Proposes a LiDAR-free, scalable data generation framework that uses SfM+MVS reconstruction and lifts manual 2D annotations to 3D, requiring annotation of only <10% of images while covering >99% of reconstructed points.

The dataset is substantial for the aerial domain: 9 scenes, >20k samples, ~193,938 m^2, 21 semantic classes, multiple altitudes (30/40/50 m), seasons, and urban/industrial/rural environments, with RGB images, semantic voxel grids, metric depth maps, and masks.

Provides useful benchmarking evidence: validates reconstruction with 1.24 px average reprojection error and 92% pixel-wise agreement with manual annotations, and shows a clear domain gap for both SSC and monocular depth foundation models.

The benchmark experiments are informative: SSC methods achieve very low mIoU (~2%), and depth models improve substantially after fine-tuning on OccuFly, supporting the paper's claim that aerial 3D understanding is underexplored.
Well organized and largely clear, with extensive supplementary details on data generation, class distributions, implementation parameters, altitude-wise evaluation, and qualitative results.
weaknesses: Scene-level diversity is limited: all 9 scenes come from the broader Ingolstadt, Germany region, and the train/val/test split is only 5/2/2 scenes. Despite 20k samples, the benchmark may not test geographic generalization or global aerial diversity.

Evaluation breadth is modest: SSC is benchmarked with only two methods (Symphonies and DISC), and there is no aerial-specific baseline, no multi-altitude fusion baseline, and no oracle/ceiling analysis to contextualize the extremely low mIoU.

Ground-truth quality depends on SfM/MVS reconstruction, majority voting/kNN label transfer, and manual annotation of a subset of frames. The static-scene assumption suppresses dynamic objects, and cross-altitude temporal inconsistencies are acknowledged; the 92% agreement is measured on rendered views rather than independent 3D semantic ground truth.

Reproducibility and accessibility are not fully demonstrated: the manuscript lacks an explicit persistent dataset/code URL, license, and access details, and the pipeline relies on commercial Agisoft Metashape plus costly manual annotation (~29 min/image over 586 images), which may hinder full reproduction.

Scale comparisons with SemanticKITTI (5x samples, 6x voxels) are somewhat apples-to-oranges: OccuFly counts per-frame aerial images, while SemanticKITTI counts LiDAR scans, and the voxel grids and scene extents differ substantially (192x128x128 vs 256x256x32).

Class imbalance is severe (e.g., building 62%, person 0.0001%, truck 0.1%), so mIoU is dominated by rare classes and may not reflect practical common-class performance. Main-paper analysis would benefit from class-balanced metrics or per-class discussion.

strengths: Targets a genuine and underexplored problem. Aerial/ low-altitude Semantic Scene Completion is largely unaddressed because LiDAR-centric SSC pipelines conflict with UAV mass, energy, and flight-regulation constraints; OccuFly is a real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark (9 scenes, ~20.6k samples, 21 classes, 193,938 m2, 30/40/50 m altitudes, urban/industrial/rural, four seasons), which is a meaningful resource for the community.

The data-generation framework is sensible and scalable in principle: geo-referenced SfM+MVS reconstruction, semantic label lifting from a small manually annotated image subset, class-aware densification (instance classes via DBSCAN plus multi-view silhouette/voxel carving, ground classes via Poisson meshing, other classes via direct voxelization), voxelization, and frustum-culled per-frame ground truth with surface/occluded/invalid masks. The output organization follows SSCBench conventions, which lowers the barrier for reuse.

The authors make a reasonable effort to document ground-truth fidelity: 1.24 px average RMS reprojection error across scenes, 135 held-out manual annotations with 92% pixel-wise agreement, a 9.17% average annotation ratio, and a supplementary with concrete hyperparameters (DBSCAN epsilon/minPts per class, Poisson depth/scale, alpha-shape alpha, K=24 virtual views), which supports reproducibility of the pipeline.

The release of 20,611 per-frame metric depth maps (vs. 1,500 for WildUAV and 829 for UseGeo) and the depth-model study (MapAnythingV1.1, Metric3Dv2, DepthAnything2/3, zero-shot vs. fine-tuned, with altitude-wise breakdowns in Tab. 12) is a useful secondary contribution, and the consistent degradation with altitude is an interesting, plausibly actionable finding for the aerial community.

The paper is generally well organized and the supplementary material (per-scene semantic point clouds/voxel grids in Fig. 6, overlap maps in Fig. 11, depth histograms in Fig. 8, annotation examples in Fig. 7) gives the reader a good sense of what the dataset actually contains.
weaknesses: Ground truth is generated and validated by the same pipeline. The 92% pixel-wise agreement compares manually annotated 2D images against labels projected from the 3D reconstruction, i.e., it measures semantic consistency of the label-lifting procedure, not the metric correctness of the voxel grid; the 1.24 px reprojection error is likewise an internal-consistency measure. There is no independent reference (e.g., RTK-surveyed targets, LiDAR, or cross-check against an external source) to validate absolute geometric/semantic ground-truth quality, even though the entire value of the benchmark rests on it. The sentence 'confirming high geometric fidelity and semantic accuracy' overstates what these two checks jointly establish.

The annotation-efficiency argument is weaker than presented. The metric rho(J) > 0.99 with |J|/N < 0.1 counts a reconstructed point as 'covered' if it appears in at least one annotated image; given the reported 67% side / 74% forward overlap, covering 99% of points with ~10% of frames is largely a by-product of the photogrammetric capture pattern rather than of the spatially stratified selection heuristic. It also does not measure label quality (occlusion, multi-view disagreement), so it is a weak proxy for 'sufficient annotation'.

Two central quantitative claims are not adequately supported and appear questionable. (i) '5x the number of samples and 6x the number of voxels compared to SemanticKITTI' is not consistent with the commonly used SemanticKITTI SSC split (~20k frames, i.e., comparable to OccuFly's 20,611 samples), and the voxel count depends on the grid specification (192x128x128 at r=0.5 m vs. 256x256x32), so a raw 6x voxel comparison is close to a definitional artifact. (ii) The 'first real-world aerial SSC benchmark' claim is not positioned against concurrent aerial 3D benchmarks that the paper itself cites (e.g., ClaraVid [3], UAV3D [90], AeroMegaPlex [75]); Section 2 discusses only terrestrial SSC datasets and never analyzes the aerial dataset landscape, so the novelty claim cannot be assessed by the reader.

The 'consistent domain gap' conclusion is supported by only two SSC methods (Symphonies, DISC), both terrestrial, with depth priors substituted, and no cross-dataset experiment (e.g., train on SemanticKITTI/SSCBench and test on OccuFly, or the reverse). Without such an experiment, the low numbers (IoU ~29.5%, mIoU ~2.0%) are equally consistent with an intrinsically hard new task as with a genuine transfer failure. There is also no aerial-specific baseline and no ablation isolating which pipeline stages (densification, voxelization, frustum culling) drive GT quality.

The pipeline assumes static scenes but the data violate this assumption: Fig. 4 explicitly marks a 'dynamic object', and urban scenes contain moving vehicles and pedestrians. No dynamic-object filtering, masking, or quantification of the resulting label noise is provided, and the issue is only acknowledged in the conclusion. This can materially corrupt voxel labels (ghosting/smearing in the SfM+MVS reconstruction) in exactly the scenes that carry most of the semantic diversity. The cross-altitude temporal inconsistency is likewise acknowledged but unquantified.

The 21-class taxonomy is undermined by extreme imbalance: per Tab. 7, Person is 0.0001%, Cable 0.0018%, Cable Tower 0.0047%, Crane 0.0059%, Construction 0.2741%, with more than ten classes below ~0.02%. Tab. 11 shows these are essentially never predicted, so the effective number of usable classes is far smaller than claimed and mIoU is dominated by Building/Ground/Road-like categories. The claim that the taxonomy is 'one of the most detailed to date' is therefore of limited practical value as stated.

The depth-model comparison has fairness and interpretation issues. MapAnything (a point-map model, not a metric depth model, and by the authors' own statement not fine-tunable) is evaluated zero-shot with delta_1 = 0.000 and MAE ~30 m; DepthAnything3 zero-shot has delta_1 = 0.000 yet the best SILog. These patterns are consistent with an evaluation protocol that penalizes models whose output scale is unaligned, rather than with the models genuinely failing to perceive depth. The paper should state and justify its scale-alignment/affine-invariance handling for each baseline. In addition, the fine-tuned models are evaluated on depth maps derived from the same SfM+MVS reconstruction used as training data, so part of the reported gain may reflect distribution matching rather than true metric accuracy.

Evaluation breadth and statistical grounding are thin: the test split is only two scenes (8 and 9) with 882 samples, and all altitude-wise and class-wise conclusions (Tabs. 4, 11, 12) are drawn from this small set with no variance, confidence intervals, or seed variation reported. The depth fine-tuning protocol (e.g., how the affine-invariant DepthAnything2 adaptation was performed, how many epochs, on which split) is only sketched, which limits reproducibility of the reported numbers.

Presentation and clarity issues: hyphenation artifacts ('sub-stantially', 'frus-tum'), inconsistent naming ('MapAnythingV1.1' vs. 'MapAnythingV1.1' and 'DepthAnything2- OccuFly'), and several claims in the abstract/introduction (scalability, minimal annotation, first-of-its-kind) are asserted rather than demonstrated within the paper. These are individually minor but they compound the impression that the headline claims are ahead of the evidence.
